a07.title: Onions
text: Across an Open Space Orla Barry

A public art work on Hampstead Heath
27 July - 26 September 2000

From September 1999, Orla Barry researched Hampstead Heath and the people who use it through the cycle of the seasons. Concentrating on the Heath's public Bathing Ponds and the Lido at Gospel Oak, her research comprised diary entries, notes, overheard snatches of conversation and photographs, plus contributions from people familiar with the Heath. The work resulting from Barry's research comprised signs featuring short pieces of poetic text that appeared in the wild patches on the edges of the ponds, and a free magazine, Refugees, was made in collaboration with users of the Heath and included photographs by Ruth Corney and poetry and drawings by Malvina Cheek. The project was launched at the Parliament Hill Bandstand on July 25 with 'The Green Man', a performer who provided a musical offering, and an Irish ballad singer who performed My Pheasant Lady, written by Orla Barry. However, over the weekend that the signs were installed, a group of Heath users felt the work was inappropriate and reacted to the project by removing and vandalising the signs. No signs now exist and the installation of signs in the Lido had to be cancelled. Refugees was distributed until the end of the summer by volunteers on the Heath.

Orla Barry was born in Ireland and now lives and works in Belgium and Ireland. She studied in Dublin, Belfast, and at De Ateliers, Amsterdam. Solo exhibitions include The Scavenger's Daughter at Shed im Eisenwek, Frauenveld, Switzerland, 1999 and A Barmaids Notebook 1991-98 at Gasworks Gallery, London 1999. Her work has been prominent in numerous group shows including Manifesta, Luxembourg, 1997 and Linguistic Islands, Watou 2000, Belgium, curated by Jan Hoet.
Project supported by the Corporation of London.

a15.title: Mecca
text: Untitled (America) 1994/95 Felix Gonzalez-Torres

Lymington Road, London NW3
19 May - 16 July 2000

Untitled (America) 1994/95 comprised garlands of lights installed across a street opposite the Centre. Like all Gonzalez-Torres' work, the piece is on one level concerned with the intersecting dialogues between the realms of public and private, social and personal. Its intention is also as a decorative and celebratory piece. Gonzalez-Torres died in 1996 and a large exhibition of his work took place at the Serpentine Gallery, with other satellite projects through the duration of this project.
Gonzalez-Torres exhibited widely in America and Europe and showed alongside Ad Reinhardt and Joseph Kosuth in Symptoms of Interference, Conditions of Possibility at Camden Arts Centre in 1994.
Organised by Camden Arts Centre in partnership with the Serpentine Gallery. Supported by Edwin Cohen and Andrea Rosen.

a18.title: Contact
text: Conversation between Paul Collett, Arts Development Officer from Camden Council (Camden Arts & Tourism) and Amy Plant

Paul: I don't really have an overall image of the project to take away. I kind of had one when it began because it was originally going to be centred around the North London Line and that became very, very difficult... just because of the relationships with Railtrack and the people that run the line. It was difficult to pin them down to the timetable, so Peter Cross (the curator) had to re-think it, and it became more about the communities that live along that route, and did not directly use the stations. It was a pity because that was a tangible thread between those communities, and I think something was lost...that physical thread, that physical angle. So to my mind they became a bit too disparate perhaps as projects. Again, that's my perception coming from the outside. I was involved in the beginning, working with Camden Arts Centre in coming up with the project. I would later occasionally hear about some of the problems or...I would get the publicity and I would come to the events and I would get updates at trustees meetings, things like that... so I've got this fractured perspective which isn't good or bad, it's just a different perspective.
Amy: And also, how long have you been working in this department?
Paul: I've been at Camden for years and years. And I suppose in the public art area, working seriously for about ten.
Amy: So you've got a good experience then of this area and...

Paul: I suppose so. I'm aware of what the pitfalls are likely to be and sometimes I'm not surprised when things do go awry and sometimes with the nature of these projects you have to work with those problems and those opportunities and tease out solutions ... it's easier with some of the participants than with others.
Amy: I think it's important in public art projects to remain very flexible because you are negotiating with people who don't necessarily have an interest or an involvement in contemporary art.

Paul: Yes, you are often introducing them to new practices, new ways of working. Often they don't have the context in which to frame it themselves. So in a way Peter did really well when he rescued the project because it could have seriously floundered when the stations pulled out, and he was able to re-structure it. I've tried to identify common themes. Have you identified any common themes within the projects?

Amy: Well that's what my website is about, in fact. That's how I've focused. From the beginning, when I was asked to do this, I thought, 'O.K., It's supposed to be about some kind of links and it's not about the rail line any more,' so I thought, 'Maybe it would be interesting at the end of the projects to see what links have actually emerged' and so rather than the website being structured project by project, it's actually structured thematically. I've fixed on seven themes, because there are seven projects, so that's a kind of random number.

They've ended up being quite broad themes and they've not come from me looking at the projects, they've come from the reactions I've had from the audiences. So it's been a bit like qualitative research. So I go out and try and find out what's going on and then from that I assess it and categorise. So it's been a process of going through these conversations, picking out quotes and trying to see the overall threads. I think what's been interesting about the projects, when you talk to the audiences, is how they work as catalysts for the audiences to think about things which are happening in their local area or things that are happening in their lives generally and that for me... I found that the interesting outcome of going and talking to people. Because it almost gives another dimension to the work... it's read on a different level.

Paul: I think Peter's been quite clever in the way that he's selected the artists to work on it. Their artistic practice shares these concerns, it's not going in with something fixed, it's about whatever comes out of the conversation they have with that group of people.
Amy: In most cases. I think some of the projects had more direct involvement and were more engaging with people than others.
Paul: Can you name them all? I'm wondering if I can.
Amy: Seven is actually a really hard amount to remember. The first project was Anna Best's Mecca at the Kilburn Bingo Hall.
Paul: Yes, I saw that one.
Amy: The next one, I think, was the project with Christine and Irene Hohenbüchler.
Paul: I saw the outcome of that.
Amy: You saw the exhibition at Camden Arts Centre? What did you think of that?

Paul: I think there was an attempt to make more of the material than was actually there. I wasn't sure that an exhibition was the appropriate format for that work. The magazine was better. And from what I gathered, the project had been very problematic in terms of establishing a relationship with the user s. Obviously they're going to be suspicious, 'What are you doing with us? And what are youdoing with our material?' The difficulty of re-presenting it in an artspace. And I think perhaps it looked too much like an exhibition for an art space than...that I found quite difficult ... the way it was exhibited stopped people from seeing the work, which I thought was an issue.

Amy: Normally how those artists work is that they get the participants to be very much involved in the process of the installation. And it really fell down in that respect. And I think that's partly to do with timing and not having enough time to allow for the flexibility that's needed when it's not a conventional exhibition.

Paul: That is also reflected in the Orla Barry project. I think again, because you can't control environments in the public domain and you have more control in the white cube. Certainly more than you have on Hampstead Heath or in an art therapy class for example. That's why I think these opportunities are really exciting. Perhaps sometimes they are constrained by exhibition timetables, or the traditional framework of doing things ...it doesn't have to follow an exhibition format. And projects should be allowed, in fact, to go off in other directions. But it's incredibly difficult to achieve, because you've got to keep everyone on board, you've got to keep your staff on board, you've got to keep the funders on board... At the end of the day everyone wants an outcome, they want something tangible. And often you have to simply guess what these tangible outcomes could be... and the Centre in this instance wanted an exhibition and perhaps it wasn't appropriate. It's difficult. But I think you're right, I think it's been a real eye opener...to be directly involved in those issues. They took on a lot, you know.

Amy: I thought that seven projects was too ambitious. If they had done less the artists could have been better resourced and supported. And what about what Maurice did? I was very interested in his approach...he was very intangible I thought, or could be seen as that way. 'Are we going to get any results?!' Lots of ideas, but nothing's confirmed yet. And for Maurice, that really wasn't a problem... the idea of the project for him was that he was working all the time...

Paul: I actually thought he was a good choice. I would love to work with him within the Council, but it would possibly be the last project that I ever work on because it could go anywhere. He's fantastic and I like what he does, I like him as an individual. Again, I'm not sure about the outcome for this project. I know that there were parts that weren't realised probably because they ran out of time... something was going to happen at the O2 Centre and something on the estate opposite...

The event he did on the Finchley Road was curious, it was surreal. I don't know, I'm a bit wary about people standing around in this context with glasses of wine... it was a close to becoming a bit of a freak show. And I don't like that. I've just been reading Sarah Kent (art critic) talking about the Gillian å Wearing private view at the Serpentine... apparently it was horrible. Why didn't the Serpentine re-think it? Why didn't they do something more in keeping? You don't have to have drinks there, have them elsewhere, or have tea and coffee, I don't know, make some allowance for the work...
Amy: Does it always have to be an art-style private view?
Paul: Exactly, the work isn't about that ... there's a jarring of conventions... so I wasn't totally convinced by what Maurice did. But I suppose I feel like that about many of the projects really.
Amy: The conventions... like you say, that are happening in galleries are suddenly brought out into the public arena...

Paul: Yes, and you cannot transpose the conventions of an art gallery onto the outside... but that is learned through experience. There are no rules. Most curators who work outside have been bred within the gallery context. I think they always get a shock on leaving it. I think it's probably good for them. But I wish that someone would take it back into the gallery, you know.
Amy: Yes, that's a very good point.

Paul: I don't think there should be rigid divisions, I think that's stupid. If you want to work with artists, you want to expose their practise, you want to get a wider audience... well, some artists are interested in that and others aren't. It's not a case of right or wrong, it's just how they work. I think the Centre genuinely believed that the project would enable them to reach new audiences and bring some of those audiences back into the Centre. Whether that has happened, whether someone has attempted to evaluate that...

Amy: I don't know actually....I mean how do you do that as well?... It's very hard to please everybody. I think the Journey's project worked brilliantly in terms of creating a close relationship with the participants.

Paul: Yes, and the library was a good setting for it. The realisation of it was very good and I think it was good for the library to see how â that kind of work can be presented professionally. I think that was one of the more successful of the projects.

Amy: And I think the participants gained a lot from it. There's no bad feelings left after that one, if you see what I mean. But on the other hand, the projects that have back-fired slightly have been massive learning curves and it's important to think of them in a positive way.
Paul: Which do you think were the more successful?

Amy: I think it's hard to gauge, because I think success in these kind of projects... someone said... ages ago, I read it in a book...that success is like the weather, it's subject to change. So it depends on what angle you look at it. Is it about making people happy? Or is it about learning something about that community or different parts of the community. And I think with the projects that have backfired, the success can maybe come later, if that's been taken on board.

Paul: Yes, it would be nice to think that with the Orla Barry one... again if there was someone around to do it...it would be painful, but you know, relations could be re-established with these people. I think Orla's words, the concept was fine...it just struck me afterwards, thinking about it, that people were probably taken aback by the physical signs ... they do look like estate agents' boards. Maybe it could have taken another form, something wrapped around the trees, I don't know, it could have said the same thing and it would have got the message across. The message didn't get across at all because they weren't up there long enough for people to see them, quite frankly...by all accounts they were down within twenty four hours. But it does show you the strength of feeling and people began writing to the local paper. Something obviously went wrong in the run up to it.

Amy: I think that was a big lack of communication. Assuming that the Corporation of London were dealing with the Pond Associations and they let them down. I mean, Orla said afterwards that she never would have put those signs up if she knew the reactions would have been as they were. So again, that's one of those things where you've got a sort of triangle going on and there's not enough communication between the different parties.

Paul: But it would be nice to think that the Centre would consider doing another project on the Heath and that they would learn form this experience. But it's difficult getting those relationships right because you're going in with hardly anything and you're calling on people's time, they're not being paid and you're asking them to become an active participant in a project that they don't know anything about and are little interested in. You've got to get them interested and that just takes time. I think when it does work it can be very exciting and rewarding for everyone involved.

Amy: Yes, and with the ponds as well...it obviously does say a lot about how people feel about that space and how it w Ðorks...it's obviously very intimate, and one person that I spoke to who's used the ponds for years... he was saying that one of the reasons people go there is to get away from the commercial signs and all that bombardment of...

Paul: The words were not commercial at all, but I think the format was, that's what grated with them, so a more subtle approach, not so 'in your face', something more intriguing coudl have been better. It's a pity though, it should have been a really nice project. It is strange how people have these perceptions of space. Hampstead Heath is public space open to anyone. The objectors do not have any legal claim on that land yet people are very territorial.
Amy: Absolutely, it's a sort of colonisation of a place isn't it?
Paul: Yes, people who come in are outsiders.

Amy: Even when I went down there I felt like an outsider, going down to the Women's Pond, and I did feel,'Oh, I shouldn't really be here'. That was interesting, yes. I di Ødn't go swimming though, it's too deep for me. I think it's also to do with people getting to know each other in a particular space as well and communities aren't necessarily defined geographically either, especially the ponds, people come from all over the place to use those. Lots of issues like that have come up through doing this project and through this process of talking to people, and one of the themes that has come out...the title for it is 'Sacred Places'... about these places where people maybe even have a spiritual connection with, especially natural environments and also in the Bingo Hall, Anna made a lot of connections between religion and gambling and that's come out as well.

Paul: I thought that was an interesting project. Again some of the finish could have been better. I think they could have had a better screen put in. Anna also used a couple of slide projectors in the foyer, and I think more could have been made of that. It was too discreet. I know s Ùhe wanted to create the illusion that these things were transient, almost magical... but people aren't used to encountering such things in that environment so you've got to be bolder. I quite liked Adam Chodzko's, I think there's something spiritual there in a way. I like the idea that you have to make an imaginative leap across continents. It was a simple yet strong idea.
Amy: And another one of the themes is about dreaming and escaping because it's all very much an escapist...
Paul: Yes, yes, and that ties in with Anna's.

Amy: Yes, it's also about escaping from boredom, I thought that's why people do go there to get away from the harsh realities of their own lives and dreaming perhaps about winning money and all the possibilities that come through that. The same with Maurice, there were a lot of dreams about the future of the Finchley Road, 'What we would like, how we would like it to be improved', that kind of thing. And the people I talked to about Adam's work, Ö most people really loved it actually, they really appreciated...I think it's worked and in a way it's a very traditional piece of public art in the sense that it's been plonked into a space but it hasn't been given a monumental-ness to it at all. Unless you notice it you would think it was the same as the other signs in the car park.

Paul: How did the Arizona connection come about? I mean with a lot of the things he does it's an act of faith isn't it? Like the material he has extracted from newspapers - has he made them up? Are we to believe that there is something out there in the desert?

Amy: Yes, I wasn't sure if it really was, but it was put there and it still should be there. If nothing's happened to it. And in fact some people are going there...they went to Arizona to do something and they went to look for the sign and I actually met some people who are moving to Arizona as well, so you never know, they might send me a picture! I met them at the O2 Centre w Ühile I was giving out cacti. Cacti, deserts, a very simple idea, but it worked. It's amazing how many people I spoke to had actually been to a desert. There must be another one we haven't talked about... let me see... Journeys...
Paul: Wasn't there one before...

Amy: Oh, Felix Gonzalez Torres! The light bulbs. I thought that worked too. Rumours had started to spread about what the lights were for and everyone was trying to guess. And all these different ideas were coming out. Some people thought it was because of the Queen Mother's birthday or the mayor getting in, all those kind of things.
Paul: Do you think that it mattered that they didn't twig it was an art work?

Amy: No, I thought that gave it a very nice dimension and I think that's partly what the artist would have wanted anyway. The idea was that if you see something like that, what does it make you think of? For me it brought up this notion of collective conscious, if you like, lots of people thinking the s áame thing at the same time, like 'Where's the street party?' It's an associative thing, to see lights like that. And I think what happened was that once I told people it was by an artist and it was to do with Camden Arts Centre, they said 'Well, if it's art, you need to explain that, if it's just light bulbs, you think of carnival, or whatever.' And then I explained to them that the artist may have wanted them to have an idea and to use their imaginations as to what it might be, and then I think they understood that, but some people felt that it would have been nice to know, maybe after they'd been up for six weeks or something, to then find out it's an artwork. I think maybe you need a balance in a situation like that. Maybe if people knew from the beginning that it was art work, all those rumours spreading maybe wouldn't happen, or they would have a different nature about them. But maybe if no one does go out there and talks to people... well maybe that's fine for it to happen å in an invisible way, absolutely. It was very interesting for me anyway...

Paul: It's important if you want to evaluate the worth of the project... the effect of the project on those people, but without actually doing this kind of qualitative assessment... and it's so time consuming.
Amy: Oh yes, it is!

Paul: I think one of the big issues with public art, because we are bombarded with so much visaul information, is how do you look at it? OK we see those lights and we've seen the Christmas lights in Regent Street, it's inevitably going to conjure those associations. I imagine that the artist still wanted to get his message across. To get people to shift their perceptions of the world through experiencing this particular physical manifestation. You want them to do that, I suppose that's what Peter wanted them to do...create the circumstances where that perceptual shift is possible. You don't want to ram it down people's throats but at the same time...it's a difficult balance to Ûstrike because of all the advertising and visual pollution you're competing with. I know that sometimes people say, 'I can't read that in the same way that I read an advert, it's not as instantaneous', but how do you encourage people to stay with it? I think that artists also have to take that on board, I think they have to make more of an allowance when they're working outside of the white cube... Another thing is scale. You know when someone's got it wrong because it just looks diminutive and you know it's not, that it has a big idea contained but somehow it's lost. But that's not to say you can't have a small object with a big impact.
Amy: In a way the light bulbs...
Paul: That worked, it was a great setting the way the road...
Amy: The gradient.
Paul: And the way it had a physical link to the Centre as well.

Amy: And it linked the two sides of the street, which was very interesting because people talked about the differences that are going on down that street, on the one hand you've got a housing estate which has lots of elderly people and people on low incomes and on the other side you've got this posh cricket club which is used by people who don't necessarily live down that street. Some of the people I spoke to there actually came from Southgate. And even when I was there, I had a camera stolen, there were police going down the road because someone was trying to commit suicide, in one of the flats and at the same time you've got this lovely sunny day and this lovely cricket game going on in the background.
Paul: Again, everything is crushed up against each other a mix of cultures, class, knowledge, education, expectations...

Amy: Definitely. In a way that project revealed that tiny area and what was going on and the animosity there and it's like a kind of microcosm in a way and I'm hoping that the website will... because I've gone into the details, very much so, individual experiences, and what's come out of that will have a global resonance, I hope.
Paul: So how many people have you spoken to?
Amy: It's between one and two hundred.
Paul: That's a lot. Did anyone turn you down? Were there places that you couldn't access?
Amy: No, only the life guards at the ponds, they wouldn't talk to me. Well she wouldn't let me record it, you see. She said that I would have to get permission from the Corporation of London.
Paul: Did you speak to them?

Amy: To the Corporation? I haven't. I haven't really gone down that road so much, I'll have a link to their website so it'll give an idea of...I had to limit myself because it could become really huge and sprawling. Paul: They are supposed to be stake holders and they weren't in the end. It would be interesting to know what they felt...I'm sure you're right, it was about lack of communication or expectations not being met on both sides. But it would be good for them actually, to take some responsibility for what happened. Amy: What do you think about the fact that a lot of people came from abroad as well? Orla was popping over from Brussels... quite sporadically.
Paul: I don't know really.
Amy: I mean my view on it, is that it's quite a luxury to have these international artists coming in and on the other hand it's, 'Well, OK, what is their relationship with this area?'

Paul: Perhaps it was too much of a leap. Maybe the Centre should have had more local artists, or a mix and then the next step would be to introduce... I don't know, it's easy to say in retrospect. Projects I've worked on have experienced similar pitfalls, ...sometimes you think you've sorted it out but you're still surprised by the reaction of people. Maybe it's just too ambitious, maybe it's just trying to achieve too much.
Amy: And what about the future?

Paul: I know the Centre is still keen to develop these kind of projects. There is going to be a period of time when the building is inaccessible during its renovation. I át will be physically closed, so again that's an opportunity to use the site, or sites nearby. Maybe they should think about doing a project that has two halves to it. One half that is defined by not knowing what the outcomes might be and the other where outcomes are more predictable ... so you keep the funders happy, you've got the press, profile, artistic credibility assured and you have this other project working in the shadows, which can take more risks. May be you get someone like Maurice who spends eighteen months there with no pressure for him to deliver an exhibition at the end.
Amy: Absolutely.

Paul: I would want them to produce something but I think it has to be something which is appropriate to the way they are working and the changing circumstances that they find themselves in over that period of time. That's your ideal project really, but it's very difficult to get that funded.

Amy: Absolutely. I have that problem. It's always the same. That's how I like to wor àk as well, but everybody wants proposals, right from the start and there isn't that room for the research. But they do residency programmes at Camden Arts Centre and I think that worked well, how they combined...some of the artists actually did residencies at the Centre. I think Anna Best used her residency also for keeping a foot in the art world, because it can be very isolating as well for artists working in different contexts.
Paul: Yes absolutely, they begin to lose their focus.

Amy: But she also brought some of her audience from Mecca into the Centre as well, she actually organised a Bingo game in the Centre. I didn't go to that unfortunately, so I'm not sure how that went, it sounded like it went very well, but I thought that was quite strange, I remember thinking at the time...I suppose it was just an exchange process, and then you had it happening in the other way as well, especially at the end of Anna's project, she had the final event at the end of the month and lots of people came from the art world, suddenly into that situation and that, I find quite an interesting...
Paul: It's interesting but can also be awkward.
Amy: Very awkward. It's awkward from both sides.
Paul: Yes, because if we're not careful we become voyeurs, that's the other way of looking at it.
Amy: Absolutely, and a lot of the art audience probably felt, 'Well, what am I doing here?', you know.
Paul: We can all go round and admire the building and admire the Wurlitzer organ but we might not associate with the people that patronise the place.
Amy: But maybe those kinds of tensions are quite useful and informative anyway.

Paul: Yes. That's the content of the work isn't it, in some way. It's just about how you involve people, again it's what's appropriate. Maybe the art world has to be on better behaviour when it's going out to...
Amy: The public, absolutely.

Paul: It can't appropriate places for ten minutes and then just walk out. It just ca ÿn't. One thing that annoys me is that you do a project in a particular place and it becomes tainted by association so you can't go back for more funding to do a further project there. OK, so Anna Best has done a project at the Kilburn State Bingo Hall, so why can't it be followed by other artists' projects.
Amy: Because it's already been done.

Paul: But that's about building and nurturing your audience. Why can't we expose these people to lots of different ways of working? That's how you build confidence by comparing and contrasting. And then you might get them then to start thinking about going to the gallery. That is interesting. I haven't fathomed out how best to do that yet.

I think the residency thing is very interesting in terms of the public art debate. The very nature of residency means that you've got someone, although not necessarily physically based in a particualr place, who has to keep going back and encountering people more than just once. And hopefully you get a conversation developing and from that that you make work that has already establsihed an audience. That's what many of these projects attempted to do. Peter had identified key audiences so I don't think the approach was wrong at all.

Amy: Someone else said to me that the work they have done has been like field work in a sense, it has kind of skimmed over things. It hasn't gone into anything very deeply but it has helped to identify the audience.

Paul: So maybe where they should go next is to identify a site and really build a long term relationshi p with that site and the communities around it. Say 'Look, we're going to work with that group or groups for the next three years, maybe just do one project a year', and then you may get those people coming to the Centre on a regular basis. It is more than just a marketing exercise, you could be very cynical and say this is just a marketing exercise, but it was never conceived as that, it was and is much more.

Amy: And even with this website, I was quite wary at times, you know, 'Am I just providing more PR for them by doing this?' and it's quite important for me and for the Centre, I think, that it's not going in that direction. Although it's not going to go into the bureaucratic details or the curatorial problems, it's supposed to be interesting for the local audience.

a26.title: Better Scenery
text: Better Scenery Adam Chodzko

Car park and lower lobby, O2 Centre, Finchley Road, London NW3
17 December 1999 - 27 August 2000

Better Scenery was an escapist proposition which connected the Arizona Desert, USA, and Finchley Road, London. In each location, a sign gave written directions to the other place. Together they suggested the possibility of travelling from the Painted Desert, in the middle of nowhere, to the urban car park of the O2 leisure centre and vice-versa. Photographs of both signs in situ were displayed in the lower lobby of the O2. Though thousands of miles apart, the signs signified an imaginary space, reflected in the backdrop of imitation rocks, water features and tropical sounds of the O2 leisure centre.

Adam Chodzko's installation continued his exploration of transitional states. He has previously conducted searches for people who think they look like God within the pages of Loot newspaper, and the 'murdered' adolescents in Pasolini's film Salu; and asked lighting technicians to stage their version of the appearance of heaven. Chodzko has exhibited widely in Britain and internationally, including the Ikon Gallery, Birmingham 1999, in Dream Machines at Camden Arts Centre and touring, 2000, and the British Academy, Rome 2000.

a35.title: Journeys
text:
Journeys Esther Sayers, Anthony O'Flaherty, Claudia Kappenberg
with members of the Deaf community

Swiss Cottage Central Library, London NW6
29 November 1999 - 30 January 2000

Journeys is a video work which follows eight individuals on their travels - real and imaginary. A collaborative project, this travelogue began as a series of practical workshops with members of the deaf community. Working together with the artists, each participant filmed and edited their own individual journey. Two commentaries act as guides; one signed by each participant in British Sign Language and another spoken. Journeys presents new ideas about conditions of access for deaf or hard of hearing people, placing them at the centre of their own experience and giving them the choice of what to communicate to a hearing audience.

Esther Sayers, Anthony O'Flaherty and Claudia Kappenberg work extensively both as artists and within art education, and are all based in London. Their individual practices include video, printmaking, photography and glasswork.
Journeys was funded by the Arts Council of England Artists in Sites for Learning Scheme and Camden Libraries and Information Services.

a51.title: On Finchley Road
text: On Finchley Road Maurice O'Connell

Midland Crescent, Finchley Road, London NW3
15-17 September 2000

In consultation and conversation with local businesses, shopkeepers and communities, Maurice O'Connell began researching possibilities for change on the Finchley Road during his residency at Camden Arts Centre in April 2000. O'Connell proposed interventions in various locations to highlight the history and development of the Finchley Road. The project itself was shaped by the artist's method of consultation with local people. These dialogues focused on Midland Crescent, a faded, mysterious gateway leading away from the incessant traffic of Finchley Road, where a gala celebration took place over a weekend, highlighting the area with bunting, strings of lights and newly painted walls. Passers by were invited to join the celebration and asked to reveal their attitudes about and ambitions for the area. The project is a starting point for future consultation and collaborative work between specific communities along Finchley Road and Camden Arts Centre.

Maurice O'Connell's work has been presented in museums, galleries and a wide range of non-gallery spaces in Ireland, the UK, Europe, South America and the USA. Notable projects include Conversations at the Castle, Atlanta, 1995; The Handpainted O, CCA, Glasgow, 1996; Tranzit, a major public art programme in Ventspil, Latvia in 1998 and in the same year, an audience development project for the Sao Paulo Biennale.

a66.title: We all peel the onions
text: Conversation between We all peel the onions participants, Paul Danvers (art therapist) and Amy Plant in the art room at the Day Hospital.
Extract 6

E: I was an out-patient and it was different for me, but if you were coming everyday to the day hospital you would have felt that your space had been taken in a way, because they were always in here. But I only came in on the Wednesday afternoons and a Thursday. Originally I think they expected us to be spontaneous and join in which I think was a problem for everyone. But I did sort of get into it. Although after coming in every Wednesday and Thursday, they were just making masks and at one point I wanted to get all these labels and write terms of mental illness on them to title them, because I didn't feel it expressed anything.

So when we went to the exhibition...some of my friends thought it was a primary school exhibition because there was no individuality and Grant's magazine, which to me was...it just didn't match up with the work, it was like two separate things. And also that they had come into a day hospital and there was no expression, I don't feel, about mental illness, it was really about masks...I suppose it was quite symbolic in a way, like putting a mask on...but...so yes, there was disappointment there.

I mean, people felt that they had been used for the project, I didn't feel that, I thought, 'They're artists and they've got to earn a crust', do you know what I mean? And that was it, I didn't mind doing it...I've been coming here for four years and to me it was something different, it was a change and it was only something that lasted so many weeks, and they were OK. There were a few misunderstandings but that could have just been language and culture.

I think it was an experience, it's just a shame that we couldn't do something that matched the magazine. Because Grant was asking all these questions about mental illness and that's bringing up stuff for us, so you're bringing up all this stuff and you're telling him and it's all printed in this magazine and then you've got this exhibition of primary school beads. There was such a huge contrast I can't imagine, people outside, what they would have made of that.

We had to hear how the twins were really vulnerable, they're in a different country, OK fair enough, but they need to realise that we too were vulnerable people coming into a day hospital, people with mental illness...moan, moan, moan, moan!
Amy: What do you think about these two different worlds meeting? Because it brings up all those questions really, should they meet, or should it just be kept separate, or...

E: I don't think it's wrong for them to meet but I think if there was more understanding about it...I just think it could have been a better experience, I don't think they shouldn't meet. But I mean there were nice things. The twins were OK. It was an odd thing to do.

a67.title: We all peel the onions
text:
We all peel the onions Christine and Irene Hohenbüchler
with participants from a Day Hospital
linked to the Royal Free Hospital NHS Trust

Camden Arts Centre, London NW3
4 February - 26 March 2000

From November through December 1999, Christine and Irene Hohenbüchler made collaborative works of art with a group of psychiatric patients at a Day Hospital linked to the Royal Free Hospital NHS Trust. They developed projects and activities that challenged and explored expectations and approaches to art and therapy, by choosing unusual materials and asking participants to produce images relating to their personal experiences. The results of these collaborations were exhibited by the Hohenbüchler sisters at Camden Arts Centre. The debate and analysis that accompanied the project resulted in a special edition of the publication Victorya, curated by Grant Watson.

The Hohenbüchler sisters have been working both together and independently for ten years, and their practice regularly extends to collaboration on multiple authorship projects, working with people living in or attending medical treatment centres (particularly in the area of mental health), educational groups or penal institutions. Recent exhibitions include Documenta X, Kassel 1997 and the Venice Biennale 1999.
The project was possible thanks to the assistance of Anthony Auerbach at the Austrian Cultural Institute, Grant Watson, Paul Danvers, Kay Thompson and the Royal Free NHS Trust.

c51.title: We all peel the onions
text: Conversation between We all peel the onions participants, Paul Danvers (art therapist) and Amy Plant in the art room at the Day Hospital.
Extract 4
Margaret: But people are marginalised like us and I think they're more marginalised because of the whole thing.
M: Yes, we've been made anonymous and we've been reduced.
Margaret: Which is what happens with people with mental health problems. It's exacerbated the problem.

M: And people probably do think that you do things like nursery school in places like this, well I mean people do tend to make assumptions about people with mental health problems which is that they are somehow backward.
K: That project is not at all a fair representation of the day-to-day work, it's completely different from the work that we do, isn't it?
M: As the only representation.
K: Yes, that's the only exhibition we've had since I've been here, a year and it's not like what goes on everyday.
Amy: And what about the magazine, Victorya, how did you feel about that?
M: I thought that was better than the exhibition.

Amy: I mean, I personally felt that it was a really good insight into...People obviously trusted Grant quite a lot, to be so lucid about their experiences, that's what I thought anyway. Reading that I found it fascinating. Not in a voyeuristic way, but I found it very honest and I got the sense that Grant had a very good presence here, simply because...
M: The interviews do show that people felt they trusted him, I think you're right about that.

K: I found the interviews good. I liked the interviews. Because you felt like you could cover your illness and all that happened. You went into a separate room and talked about the history of yourself.

Margaret: What they should have done, was make this huge, inbetween all the frippery stuff, they should have reproduced all those interviews with really big letters inbetween to show that these were grown-up people who did this, with ideas, imaginations, personalities. A human being, one that you should respect, with a lot of talent.

K: I think that people found it difficult because it's meant to be therapeutic so obviously if people weren't enjoying a task set it was continued with. It wasn't changed or altered or stopped or anything like that. So people felt that they had to go along with something that they weren't terribly into and if at the end they (the artists and organisers) were disappointed with the attitude of people here... From what I've heard... it just sounded like they were angry or upset that they'd taken trouble to do this in the art room and they hadn't had the response they wanted and they shouldn't have been expecting any specific response.
M: They didn't listen to what people were saying around them. People were saying, 'I'm not sure if I feel like doing masks' or whatever.
Paul: It was an experiment wasn't it?
K: Yes, it was an experiment.
Margaret: That's no excuse, it was an experiment! An experiment on vulnerable human beings!
Paul: What I'm saying is it's a diversion from what normally goes on here, something entirely new.

M: Well diversion's a lot nicer than the word experiment. People did feel experimented on...the people who are here were finding it very difficult to get in the door, let alone to paint something or be told to paint something and what with. I mean some people were suffering. We wouldn't be here otherwise, it's not sort of like, you know...it's not an art school.
K: That's what I mean, if it's an art school, that's fair enough. But it's not an art school.
Paul: It's not an art school, but there's a lot of creative energy here.
M: Yes, but it poses the question, are you allowed to show your suffering or are you only allowed to present to the public a happy face?
Paul: There was one guy who went to the show and said something about...and he said he really enjoyed the show and from his point of view the other show presented psychosis, the Marlene Dumas.
K: Really?
Paul: And that your bit had a sort of energy...
K: Marlene Dumas, she's not psychotic though.
Margaret: How do you know?

text: ON THE BEACH
Insouciance is one of those words you save up, waiting for exactly the right time to use it.

Eureka! My first summer in northern climes far removed from London's beloved Heath and there it was - abandoned in sand dunes along with naughty remnants of a tryst - it's colourful covers clashing with the hot golden sand and title 'REFUGEES' screaming out 'Read Me'!
Northumbria, least populated area of England, justifiably boasts miles of stunning beaches punctuated with dunes sporting wild grasses, pretty Tufted Pink Sea Thrift, Red Campion and Sea Asters.
Unique to this area, the Durham Argos butterfly may not be the only unexpected find to the inquisitive exploring adventurer in search of something 'to fill one's void'.

Travel changes your sky but not your mind............ Fast-forwarding through the pages of REFUGEES which, like a good book, provided instant optical instrument to take one away from oneself, sweet memories of invigorating days and steamy nights flooded back - faster than the incoming tide!
Oh to be on Hampstead!
I settled on the sand, shaded by tall marram grass and re-read the contents with more deliberation.
The sweetness of seclusion in such peaceful environs was shattered by a distant nearby giggle.

At 'see level' on my knees, peeping over the dune, I spotted two interacting heavenly bodies part concealed by grass, as snug as two spoons in a silver tray. Spellbound, I stared from a safe, noncommittal distance and was about to do what my conscience dictated when the couple disengaged from friendly assault and rolled apart to reveal 'Adam & Steve' as nature intended. If clothing makes a statement, such masculine nudity left me lost for words. The one with zero crop and tackle to die for smiled on seeing me before returning his attentions to the blonde 6th Former who looked like he had been reared on wild strawberries, asparagus tips, perrier water and diet dental floss! For one devoted to a religion of Eros, a devotee of Bacchus and professor of desire, here was quality eye candy - the original 'bubble-butt boy'!

A frisson of expectation wafted across the dunes like the gentle sea breeze, heralding my surprise discovery that I had chanced upon Blyth's answer to Hampstead heath or the Pere-Lachaise cemetery in Paris (where Oscar Wilde.... 'the only way to get rid of temptation is to yield to it'.......rests in his heaven).

In later conversation with another chance encounter and the assistance of my filed glasses, my findings were confirmed! - Not only Ross Gulls (that follow fishing boats from the Arctic back to the Tyne), majestic Fulmars or Puffins, but much, much more for the beach-wise adventurer to see and do.
..............a bit like the Heath, minus dendrophiles!

On my next visit to this sandy oasis away from the sounds and sights of the inhabited world, I shall assume the station of an outcast REFUGEE, devoted beyond the confines of the other world in this lonely and enchanting penance.
Who knows? I may even get picked up!
Tom Graham    August 2000

text: From Flagstaff, Arizona take route 89 northeast then route 510 east then 505 northeast for 7 miles until you reach a left turn soon after passing Moon crater. Follow this dirt track (route 244A) for 6 miles northeast passing the volcanic formations of The Sprout and the Merriam Crater on your right. Half a mile beyond a small well take the track that heads north towards Little Roden Spring. After exactly 6.9 miles a rough overgrown cinder track leads off to the left. Head west along this for a quater of a mile until you reach a fence post. Then walk 100 yards 160 degrees southeast. At this point stop and face due east (visible on the horizon are the Roden Crater and the glow of pink rocks in the Painted Desert). Situated here in this place, is a sign which describes the location of this sign you have just been reading.

e43.title: Better Scenery
text: Dear Amy,

Part of our research trip to the American deserts this summer brought us to Flagstaff to visit James Turrell's Roden Crater project. While we were in Flagstaff we searched for two days for Adam Chodzko's sign. Unfortunately we did not find it despite our concerted efforts.

On the first day we followed the instructions from the sign standing in the O2 centre. Our first problem was to find the highways, as they were not denoted by number but by destination on the signs. The Leupp road turned out to be the 510 and from there it was easy to find first turning. At this point the measurements became ambiguous; from which point should we measure? There were a number of turnings off the Leupp road but none corresponded to 7 miles from any point. After a few passes we saw that road 244A was marked at a distance closer to 9 miles from the junction. This was a cinder road, which constantly branched out into tracks leading to isolated shacks and houses. To the best of our ability we stayed on the 244A, however it led us in a north-westerly direction onto state property. As we were travelling in an estate car on these rough cinder tracks, and because of our fear of trespassing into a prohibited area we decided to turn back. In the process we sank into the cinders from which we had to push the car free.

That evening we decided not to trust the road numbers and navigate by landmarks all marked on the Ordnance Survey map we picked up at a camping store in Flagstaff. We also decided to hire a 4x4 to make the journey easier.

Driving on the cinder roads was much easier with the truck, and it did not take us long to find our way. We followed the 244A for about half a mile and then turned off in a north-easterly direction towards the Sproul (not Sprout, as spelt in the instructions). This led us to a newly conditioned road. We passed a number of small wells until we reached the one marked on the map. We also passed other noticeable landmarks, such as an alternative community. They were neither marked on the map nor mentioned in the instructions. The location of the well on the map was to the left of the road, however, in reality it lay to the right leaving us uncertain of the accuracy of the instructions. We finally arrived at Roden Springs, which marked the end of the public road going north. A locked gate prevented us following the road to Little Roden Springs. From this point we too could see the Painted Desert and the Roden Crater on the horizon.
Sadly we had to turn back and ended our two-day search for Better Scenery. On the return to the highway we discovered that this conditioned road was the construction access to the Roden Crater.
NB: We have images of the Roden Crater and of Roden Spring. Please contact us if interested.
Desert Fox
